questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a network of cracks indicates
questions.stem: In a file note on a disputed panel, the clerk records a network of fine cracks running diagonally across the painted surface. What does such a pattern usually indicate?

options.text: Movement in the panel or its layers, where the wood has responded to changes in temperature and humidity.
The underdrawing was executed with a brush that split and dragged as it was used.
options.misconception: attributes the cracking to a faulty brush in the underdrawing

options.text: The panel was painted by more than one hand, each leaving its own trail of cracks.
options.misconception: reads the crack network as evidence of several painters

options.text: The varnish has been laid too thickly and has cracked as it dried.
options.misconception: blames the varnish layer for the cracking of the panel

questions.explanation: Fine cracks that cross the painted surface point to the support moving beneath a brittle paint layer. A split brush, several painters and a faulty varnish would each leave a different kind of trace.
questions.hint: Ask what lies under the paint that could move.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute a ratio from foreshortened ceiling figures
questions.stem: The clerk's note on a ceiling panel records that the figures shrink progressively: the nearest measures 120 centimetres across the shoulders and the farthest 60. What fraction of the near figure's shoulder width is the far figure's?

options.text: Three quarters, since the far figure is 120 minus 60, a loss of 60 centimetres.
options.misconception: reports the loss as though it were the retained share

options.text: One half, since 60 divided by 120 gives 0.5 of the near shoulder width.
One third, since the far figure is judged by eye to be a third of the near one.
options.misconception: estimates the ratio from appearance rather than measurement

options.text: Two thirds, since the difference has been measured against the near width.
options.misconception: measures the difference against the near width instead of the far

questions.explanation: The far figure is 60 centimetres across against 120 for the near one, so it is one half of the near width. That halving is the effect of foreshortening on a surface seen from below.
questions.hint: Divide the far measurement by the near measurement.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tacking margins of a stretched canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the slack canvas margins
questions.stem: A question in the file asks why the margins of a stretched canvas are left loose rather than pulled tight over the frame. Explain what the loose margins are for.

answer.exemplar: The margins are the unstretched edges of the canvas, and they are left slack so that the tension of the tacks, the stretcher and any movement in the timber are taken up in the edge rather than in the painted area. If the canvas were pulled tight to the frame all round, changes in size would put strain directly on the paint layer and the picture would crack. The margins also give the restorer a grip for re-stretching.

questions.explanation: The slack edge absorbs the movement of the timber and keeps that strain away from the brittle paint. A canvas pulled tight to the frame would pass every change in size straight into the picture.
questions.hint: Think about where the strain of movement is absorbed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a factor between two fixing times
questions.stem: A file note records that a photographic plate was fixed for 5 minutes in the first batch and 9 minutes in the second, both reaching the same clear tone. By what factor has the fixing time been increased?
questions.explanation: The second batch's 9 minutes divided by the first batch's 5 minutes gives a factor of 1.8, so the longer bath stopped the action of light on the plate more thoroughly. A fixing bath arrests the change that light begins.
questions.hint: Divide the longer time by the shorter one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a varnish does and what removing it costs
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of a discoloured varnish

stimulus.body: File note on exhibit 14: the clerk records that the panel carries a yellowed varnish laid over the paint, that the picture beneath appears saturated and strongly coloured where the varnish is thinner along the upper edge, and that a restorer has valued the work far higher if the discoloured layer is removed.

questions.stem: According to the file note, what has the varnish done to the picture?

options.text: It is a later addition that has damaged the paint layer underneath it.
options.misconception: claims the varnish has damaged the paint rather than altered its appearance

options.text: It is original to the panel and should be preserved because it belongs with the work.
options.misconception: treats the varnish as part of the work rather than as an added layer

options.text: It has yellowed and darkened the colours, so removing it would reveal the work as it was painted.
It is a protective layer that improves the colours of the picture beneath it.
options.misconception: believes varnish improves rather than disturbs the colours

questions.explanation: Where the varnish is thin the colours are strong, and where it is thick they are dulled, which is the classic sign of a yellowed coating altering appearance. The note does not record damage to the paint or a protective benefit.
questions.hint: Compare the thick and thin areas of the coating.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the sequence of working a hard stone
questions.stem: A note on a carved memorial records that the mason worked the block with a hammer and point before finishing with finer abrasives. First say what the rough stage does, then say why the change of tool matters.

options.text: It marks the final measurements, and the change of tool records the mason's signature on the block.
options.misconception: invents a signature function for the tool change

options.text: It establishes the polish of the surface, and the change of tool makes the block larger rather than smaller.
options.misconception: describes the rough stage as a polish and reverses the effect of the tools

options.text: It tests the stone for flaws, and the change of tool decides the colour of the finished work.
options.misconception: assigns a colour decision to the change of tool

options.text: It removes the unwanted bulk and establishes the form, and finer tools refine it without splitting the stone.

questions.explanation: The hammer and point take away the bulk and set the mass of the work, and only then can abrasives be used to refine it without the risk of splitting. Testing, colouring and signing are not what this sequence of tools accomplishes.
questions.hint: Ask what has to exist before a surface can be refined.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define direct carving and distinguish it from casting
questions.stem: A file note on a statue contrasts it with works modelled in clay and then cast. What distinguishes direct carving from that process?

options.text: The sculptor makes the model larger than life and casts it in a cheaper metal.
options.misconception: reframes direct carving as a change of casting material

options.text: The sculptor works the final material itself, cutting the form directly out of the stone or wood.
The sculptor transfers a small drawing onto the block and cuts only the outlines.
options.misconception: reduces direct carving to cutting outlines from a drawing

options.text: The sculptor assembles the figure from separately carved parts that are later joined.
options.misconception: describes assembly rather than carving the block directly

questions.explanation: In direct carving the material of the work is cut by the sculptor, so the form grows out of the block. A model and a cast, a traced outline and an assembly of parts are three different procedures.
questions.hint: Ask what material the sculptor's tool actually meets.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of cracks in one location
questions.stem: The clerk's note on exhibit 6 records 40 cracks in the panel's upper left corner and 10 across the rest of the surface. What percentage of the recorded cracks lie in the upper left corner?

options.text: Seventy-five per cent, since the total has been rounded from 50 to 53 cracks.
options.misconception: divides by a rounded total that the note does not give

options.text: Twenty per cent, since the 10 cracks elsewhere have been taken as the corner's share.
options.misconception: reports the complement of the corner share

options.text: Eighty per cent, since 40 of the 50 recorded cracks lie in that corner.
Ninety per cent, since the corner figure has been divided by the 10 outside it.
options.misconception: divides the corner count by the count outside it

questions.explanation: There are 40 cracks in the corner and 10 elsewhere, so 50 in all, and 40 over 50 is 80 per cent. Such a concentration points to a local fault rather than general movement of the panel.
questions.hint: Add the two counts, then take the corner as a share of the total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a ceiling is composed for a viewer below
questions.stem: A claimant complains that the figures in a painted ceiling look as though seen from the floor. Explain how a painter makes a ceiling work for a viewer lying beneath it.

answer.exemplar: A ceiling is painted for a viewer below, so the figures are built with that position in mind: they are foreshortened as though seen from a point on the floor, and their positions are arranged to read from that single viewpoint. The bodies are turned so that the underside, the folds and the limbs nearest the viewer are shown, and the whole is composed as a single field read from below rather than as a scene seen at eye level.

questions.explanation: A ceiling is met by the eye at a steep angle from underneath, so bodies must be foreshortened and composed for one viewpoint below. The complaint describes the correct effect of that arrangement, not a fault in it.
questions.hint: Think about where the eye of the viewer is when a ceiling is seen.

questions.stem: A file note records that a canvas measures 120 centimetres across the painted area and that the loose margin on each side measures 6 centimetres. What is the total width of the unstretched canvas in centimetres?

questions.hint: Add the margin from both sides to the painted width.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stages described in a photographic note

stimulus.body: File note on the photographic exhibits: the clerk records that a negative of the panel was made by exposing a plate through a lens to the light reflected from the picture, that the exposure was stopped by covering the lens, and that the plate was then washed so that the image no longer changed when light fell on it.

questions.stem: According to the file note, how was the image made permanent on the plate?

options.text: The plate was coated with coloured dust which held the picture as a tinted surface.
options.misconception: confuses the fixing of an image with its colouring by a pigment

options.text: The plate was exposed to the light indefinitely and then developed by cooling it.
options.misconception: describes an unlimited exposure and an incorrect developing process

options.text: The image was copied by hand onto the plate from a drawing made of the picture.
options.misconception: turns the photographic process into a hand copying exercise

options.text: The light was allowed to act on the plate for a set time and then stopped and washed.

questions.explanation: The note describes the three stages of making an image permanent: exposure for a set time, stopping the action of light, and washing the plate. Hand copying and coloured dust are not photographic processes at all.
questions.hint: Follow the order of the stages recorded in the note.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a varnish does and what removing it costs
questions.learningObjective: State the benefit and the cost of removing a varnish
questions.stem: A note records that a restorer proposes to remove a discoloured varnish from an exhibit. First say what the varnish does for the picture, then say what removing it costs.

options.text: It fixes the paint into the panel, and removing it means the picture can never be cleaned again.
options.misconception: credits the varnish with fixing the paint into the wood

options.text: It protects and deepens the colours, and removing it leaves the surface unprotected and alters the appearance buyers know.
It makes the panel water tight, and removing it means the wooden support must be replaced.
options.misconception: credits the varnish with making the panel water tight

options.text: It records the date of the picture, and removing it destroys the only evidence of the date.
options.misconception: treats the varnish as a dated record rather than a coating

questions.explanation: A varnish protects the paint surface and gives it a slight shine that deepens the colours, and taking it off both exposes the paint and changes the appearance the market has known. Fixing paint into the wood and waterproofing the panel are not what a varnish does.
questions.hint: Ask what the restorer would gain and what the owner would lose.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why stone is worked by impact and abrasion
questions.stem: Why does a mason shape a hard stone by grinding and pecking rather than by cutting it with a fine blade as though it were wood?

options.text: Because polishing a stone with abrasives is quicker than any method of cutting.
options.misconception: claims the abrasive method is faster than carving

options.text: Because a fine blade cannot reach the interior of a block that is worked on all sides.
options.misconception: gives a geometric rather than a material reason

options.text: Because stone is brittle and cannot be parcelled, so it must be removed by impact and abrasion.
Because hard stone has no grain, so a blade would split the block in an even line.
options.misconception: invents a fault in stone that does not exist

questions.explanation: Stone fractures rather than parting, so it is removed by driving a point into it or by grinding it away with abrasive. Speed, reach and grain are not what makes a blade useless on stone.
questions.hint: Think about how a stone fails when it is cut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the stone remaining after carving
questions.stem: The clerk's note on exhibit 22 records that a carved figure was begun in a block of 180 kilograms of stone and that 150 kilograms of waste were removed, leaving the finished work and the offcuts together. How many kilograms remain?

options.text: Twenty kilograms, since a further kilogram has been subtracted without being recorded.
options.misconception: applies an extra subtraction not required by the note

options.text: One hundred and fifty kilograms, since the waste has been reported instead of the remainder.
options.misconception: reports the waste rather than the remainder

options.text: Two hundred and ten kilograms, since the waste has been added to the weight of the block.
options.misconception: adds the waste to the block instead of subtracting it

options.text: Thirty kilograms, since 180 minus 150 leaves 30 kilograms of stone in total.

questions.explanation: Subtracting the 150 kilograms of waste from the 180 kilogram block leaves 30 kilograms, which is the finished figure and its offcuts together. The note gives no grounds for any further deduction.
questions.hint: Subtract the waste from the weight of the block.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a crack pattern can and cannot establish
questions.stem: An expert is asked to write a note on why a panel has cracked in a pattern. Explain what the pattern of cracks can and cannot establish.

answer.exemplar: A network of fine cracks that follows the grain and crosses from panel to ground indicates movement: the timber has expanded and contracted more than the brittle paint layer on it can follow, and the paint has opened along the tension. Such a pattern can show that the fault is structural rather than a single impact, but by itself it cannot say when the movement happened or who was responsible, so it must be read together with the rest of the file.

questions.explanation: The pattern indicates that the support has moved beneath the paint, which is a conclusion about mechanism. It says nothing about timing or responsibility, and the expert must be careful to keep those apart.
questions.hint: Ask what a pattern of cracks records and what it cannot record.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a ratio between a ceiling field and its figures
questions.stem: A file note on a ceiling records that the painted field is 60 metres long and that the nearest figure is drawn at 4 metres while the farthest is at 2 metres. What is the ratio of the near figure's size to the far figure's?
questions.explanation: The nearer figure is drawn at 4 metres and the farther at 2, so the ratio is 4 divided by 2, which is 2. A ceiling foreshortens its figures, and the ones seen most steeply are the smallest.
questions.hint: Divide the near figure's size by the far figure's size.

questions.topic: Tacking margins of a stretched canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain what slack margins show about a painting's condition

stimulus.body: File note on exhibit 9: the clerk records that the canvas is stretched on a wooden stretcher and fixed with iron tacks along the edges, that the tacks stand well away from the painted surface, and that the unpainted margins between the picture and the tacks have folded and creased.

questions.stem: What does the condition of the margins recorded in the note tell you?

options.text: That the picture was never stretched properly and must be stretched and reworked.
options.misconception: reads the slack margins as a fault in the original stretching

options.text: That the slack margins have absorbed the movement, so the strain falls on the folds rather than on the paint.
That the margins were left by the original maker so the canvas could be removed for transport.
options.misconception: invents a transport reason for the unstretched margins

options.text: That the slack margins have caused the paint to lift away from the canvas in the centre.
options.misconception: reverses the effect, claiming the margins caused the lifting

questions.explanation: The folding of the unpainted margins is exactly what slack edges do when the support moves, and it shows the strain being taken there instead of in the picture. Poor stretching, transport margins and lifting paint are not what the note describes.
questions.hint: Ask why the folded edges are a sign of good condition.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what an exposure preserves and what it omits
questions.stem: A note records that the photographic negative of an exhibit was made by letting light fall on a plate for a fixed time and then stopping it. First say what the exposure fixes, then say what the exposure cannot preserve.

options.text: It fixes the size of the subject on the plate, and it cannot preserve any detail of the surface.
options.misconception: claims detail is lost although outlines are recorded

options.text: It fixes the colour of the subject into the plate, and it cannot preserve the outlines of the subject.
options.misconception: credits the exposure with recording colour and denies outlines

options.text: It fixes the light that fell on the plate into a permanent image, and it cannot preserve colour, since it records light alone.
It fixes the moment of viewing for the court, and it cannot preserve the object at all.
options.misconception: treats the exposure as evidence about the viewing rather than the object

questions.explanation: An exposure fixes light as an image, and because it records light rather than wavelengths it cannot preserve colour as such. Outlines, detail and relative tone are all recorded, and the object itself is preserved on the plate.
questions.hint: Ask what the plate actually measures.

questions.topic: What a varnish does and what removing it costs
questions.learningObjective: State the chief purpose of a varnish
questions.stem: What is the chief practical purpose of the varnish applied over a finished painting?

options.text: To make the picture water proof so that it may be hung in a damp room.
options.misconception: claims varnish makes a picture waterproof

options.text: To fix the paint layer permanently so that it can never be scratched.
options.misconception: overstates what varnish does to the paint's stability

options.text: To record the name of the painter and the date of the work in a legible inscription.
options.misconception: treats varnish as a documented inscription

options.text: To protect the paint surface from dirt, handling and light, and to deepen its colours.

questions.explanation: A varnish is a sacrificial protective film that also gives the surface a slight shine and so deepens the colours. It cannot fix paint into the panel, inscribe a name or waterproof the support.
questions.hint: Ask what the coating stands between the picture and the world.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the stone removed over several hours
questions.stem: A file note on a memorial records that the mason removed 3 kilograms of stone from the block in the first hour and 5 kilograms in each of the next two hours. How many kilograms had been removed after three hours?

options.text: Ten kilograms, since only the two later hours have been counted.
options.misconception: omits the first hour from the total

options.text: Thirteen kilograms, since 5 plus 5 plus the first hour's 3 comes to 13.
Fifteen kilograms, since the first hour's 3 kilograms has been counted as 5.
options.misconception: uses the later rate for the first hour as well

options.text: Eight kilograms, since the later hours have been averaged rather than added.
options.misconception: averages the hours instead of adding them

questions.explanation: Adding the three hours gives 3 plus 5 plus 5, which is 13 kilograms of stone removed. The first hour was slower because the mason was still establishing the form.
questions.hint: Add the three hours, using the right figure for each.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define direct carving and identify its traces
questions.stem: A dispute turns on whether a statue was carved directly or copied from a model. Explain what direct carving means and what its traces show.

answer.exemplar: Direct carving means the sculptor works the final stone or wood itself, cutting the form as the material gives way under the tool, so the shape grows out of the block rather than being reproduced from a separate model. Its traces are visible in the facets of the chisel, in the changes of direction the carver was willing to make, and in passages where the block's own shape has been allowed to survive. A copy made from a model tends to be more uniform and less alert to the material.

questions.explanation: Direct carving means the material of the work is cut by the sculptor and the block's own shape is allowed to influence the result, which leaves tool facets and surviving passages of the original block. A version made from a model tends to be more uniform.
questions.hint: Think about what the block's own shape does to the result.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the sequence of working a hard stone to a finish
questions.stem: A note is required on how a mason brings a hard stone to a finished surface. Explain the sequence of working and why the order of it matters.

answer.exemplar: The mason first removes the bulk with a heavy hammer and point, breaking the block down and establishing the form in rough; the point's small contact allows the stone to be driven without splitting it. Finer abrasives then follow, taking the surface down in stages from the marks of the tools to a smooth finish. Each stage must be finer than the last, because a coarse tool scored into a fine surface will reopen the damage the finer work had removed.

questions.explanation: Rough work establishes the form, and graded abrasives then remove the marks of each earlier stage in turn, so the order of the tools decides how good the final surface can be. A coarse cut made after a fine polish would undo that polish.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a coarse tool touches a fine surface.

questions.topic: What a varnish does and what removing it costs
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a varnish does and the cost of its removal
questions.stem: A restorer's report is required on a picture whose varnish has discoloured. Explain what a varnish does for a painting and what removing it involves.

answer.exemplar: A varnish is a protective film that keeps dirt, handling and light off the paint surface and that also deepens the colours by giving the surface a slight shine. Removing a discoloured varnish means taking off the whole layer with solvents, and this exposes the paint to handling again while changing the appearance that owners, dealers and buyers have known for generations. The removal therefore restores the picture but alters the object that has circulated in the trade.

questions.explanation: A varnish protects the paint and deepens its colours, and removing it means the surface is unprotected and the picture looks different from the object the market has known. The restorer must weigh a restoration against an alteration of the object.
questions.hint: Consider what the coating does and what is lost when it goes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh evidence for direct carving against alternatives

stimulus.body: File note on exhibit 18: the clerk records that the statue was carved from a single block by a carver working with hammer and chisel, that the tool marks run directly across the form without the intermediate stage of a model, and that the shape of the original block can still be traced in the lower part of the figure.

questions.stem: What does the evidence recorded in the note support?

options.text: It supports a cast work, since the smooth continuous surface proves the figure was cast.
options.misconception: reads a smooth surface as proof of casting

options.text: It supports direct carving, since the tool marks follow the block and no model stage is recorded.
It supports a figure assembled from parts, since the seams would show in the lower block.
options.misconception: invents seams that the note does not record

options.text: It supports a copy from a smaller model, since the block shape was transferred exactly.
options.misconception: reads the survival of the block shape as proof of copying

questions.explanation: Tool marks running straight across the form with the block's shape still visible and no model stage recorded is the classic evidence of direct carving. A smooth cast surface, hidden seams and an exactly transferred block shape are all absent from the note.
questions.hint: Weigh up what the note records and what it does not.

options.misconception: reads the pattern as evidence of the painting process

options.text: It suggests a single blow struck from the front, and it cannot establish whether one hand painted the panel.

questions.explanation: An even network across the whole surface points to general movement of the support, but a pattern records mechanism rather than timing or responsibility. A single blow, a wet ground and a failed varnish would each leave a different kind of trace.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a photographic record adds to a file
questions.stem: An expert is asked to explain why a photographic record of a painting shows things a witness cannot see. Explain what an exposure records and what it adds to a file.

answer.exemplar: An exposure records the light that an object reflects, so it fixes the appearance of that object at a stated moment, with any lens and any lighting of the scene recorded as well. In a dispute it can add detail that a witness could not supply, such as the state of a surface, the shape of a crack or the exact colour of a varnish, provided the record is tied to the object and the circumstances are declared.

questions.explanation: A photographic record fixes how an object appeared at a stated moment, including details that a verbal witness cannot convey. Its weight as evidence still depends on being properly tied to the object and its circumstances being declared.
questions.hint: Think about what the plate measures and what it cannot show.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a pointed tool is used before finer work

stimulus.body: File note on exhibit 27: the clerk records that the mason first worked the block with a heavy hammer and a pointed tool, that the block's sharp corners were reduced while the broad planes of the form were set out, and that the pointed tool was used because a wide edge would have split the stone.

questions.stem: According to the note, why was the pointed tool used first?

options.text: Because the block was polished with the point before the form was begun.
options.misconception: describes the rough stage as a polish

options.text: Because its small contact removes stone without splitting it, which is why it precedes any finer work.
Because the stone was too soft to take any finer tool.
options.misconception: claims the stone was too soft for a finer tool

options.text: Because the point was used to mark out the design, which was then carved from a model.
options.misconception: misreads the tool work as the transfer of a design

questions.explanation: The note gives the reason directly: a wide edge would split the stone, and the point concentrates the blow so that the block can be reduced safely. Polishing, softness and marking out are not what the point was doing.
questions.hint: Notice what the note says a wide edge would have done.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare direct carving with casting and read the evidence
questions.stem: An expert report must distinguish a directly carved statue from a cast copy. First say how the process differs, then say what in the work itself reveals which process was used.

options.text: The work is assembled from parts, and the joints between the parts reveal the process.
options.misconception: describes assembly rather than the difference between carving and casting

options.text: The carver follows a model exactly and then corrects it by hand, and only the polish reveals the process.
options.misconception: makes the two processes nearly identical and hides the evidence

options.text: The carver shapes the block itself rather than following a model, and the tool facets and surviving block shape reveal it.
The work is carved from a single block in either case, and only the records reveal the process.
options.misconception: claims the surface gives no evidence at all

questions.explanation: Direct carving means the block is cut by the sculptor, leaving tool facets and passages where the original shape of the stone survives, while a cast copy reproduces a model more uniformly. The surface itself is the chief evidence in a report.
questions.hint: Ask what the tool and the block leave behind.

options.misconception: invents a repair history from a crack pattern

options.text: The first means the picture was painted badly, while the second means the picture was painted well.
options.misconception: reads a structural fault as a matter of skill

options.text: The first suggests movement in the panel itself, while the second is a fault of the paint layer alone.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tacking margins of a stretched canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the untacked canvas margins
questions.stem: An expert must explain the purpose of the untacked margins of a stretched canvas. Explain what they do and why they matter to the survival of the picture.

answer.exemplar: The margins are the edges of the canvas that run beyond the painted area and beyond the line of tacks, and they are left slack on purpose. The timber of a stretcher and the canvas move together, but the paint on top of the canvas is brittle and cannot follow that movement, so the slack edge takes up the strain instead. Without the margin the strain would pass straight into the paint and open cracks across the picture.

questions.explanation: The margin is a deliberate buffer between the moving support and the brittle paint, and it is where the strain is absorbed. A picture without that buffer would crack as the timber responded to the seasons.
questions.hint: Think about which part of the picture cannot absorb movement.

questions.explanation: The first plate received 15 seconds and the second 10, so the second needs 15 divided by 10, which is 1.5 times the exposure to reach the same density. Equal densities on the two plates mean equal light on the plate.
questions.hint: Divide the longer exposure by the shorter one.

The old photograph has faded, and the proposal is to restore the varnish to its earlier colour.
options.misconception: blames the photograph for the change in the varnish

questions.hint: Look at the comparison with the old record and at the proposed test.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the tools of a stonemason become finer in turn
questions.stem: A note describes a mason working a hard stone first with a hammer and then with abrasives. First say why the abrasive stage follows the hammer, then say what the sequence guarantees.

options.misconception: mistakes the sequence for a description of handling and transport

options.text: Because the hammer is used only for decoration, and the sequence guarantees a polish in a single pass.
options.misconception: assigns the hammer to decoration and misstates what the sequence achieves

options.text: Because abrasives cannot be used on a carved surface, and the sequence guarantees the form will not shift.
options.misconception: claims abrasives cannot touch a carved surface

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the viewpoint changes a ceiling design
questions.stem: A note is needed explaining why a painted ceiling is not simply a wall picture turned upwards. Explain what the viewpoint changes and how a painter answers it.

answer.exemplar: A ceiling is seen from a point below it, at a steep angle, and the eye meets the surface from underneath rather than in front of it. The painter therefore foreshortens the bodies so that they appear to lie along the plane, arranges the limbs and drapery so that their undersides show, and composes the whole for the one point from which the ceiling will be seen. Turning a wall picture upwards would give the viewer figures that appear to stand on nothing.

questions.explanation: The viewpoint below changes everything about how the bodies are drawn and how the composition is arranged, and the whole is composed for a single point. A wall design turned upwards would leave figures appearing to stand on the ceiling.
questions.hint: Think about where the eye of the viewer actually is.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a photographic process from a file note

questions.stem: What process does the file note describe?

options.misconception: mistakes the plate's fixing for fixing it to the camera

options.text: The panel was copied by hand onto the glass, which was then fixed so the drawing would not fade.
options.misconception: turns the photographic process into a hand copying exercise

options.text: Light from the panel was allowed through the lens onto a plate for a measured time and the result was made permanent.

questions.explanation: A plate in a camera, a lens uncovered for a measured time and a plate developed and washed is the making of a photographic negative. Hand copying, an undeveloped plate and a plate fixed to the camera are not what the note records.
questions.hint: Follow the order of the steps in the note.

questions.topic: What a varnish does and what removing it costs
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a second layer of varnish
questions.stem: A restorer reports on a picture that has been varnished twice. First say what a varnish does, then say what the second layer changes for the viewer.

options.text: It records the date of the work, and a second layer gives an earlier and more certain date.
options.misconception: treats varnish as a dated record

options.text: It protects and deepens the colours, and a second layer darkens the picture further and makes removal harder.
It fixes the paint to the panel, and a second layer makes the paint bond more strongly to the wood.

options.text: It polishes the surface, and a second layer gives the picture a finer shine without changing its colour.
options.misconception: describes polish only and denies the change of colour

questions.explanation: A varnish protects the surface and deepens the colours, and a second coat adds another layer that darkens the picture and hardens the coating against removal. Neither dating nor bonding paint to the wood is what a layer of varnish does.
questions.hint: Ask what a second coating adds to the appearance and to the work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why rough work must precede a fine finish
questions.stem: A mason says that a piece of stone must be worked rough before it can be brought to a finish. Why is that so?

options.text: Because the rough stage allows the mason to judge the natural grain of the block.
options.misconception: gives a reason about the grain rather than about the tool marks

options.text: Because a stone cannot hold a fine finish until the outer skin has been removed.
options.misconception: invents a surface skin that must come off

options.text: Because the marks of a coarse tool will reopen any scratches left by a finer one, so the stages must get finer in turn.
Because the weight of the finished block must be roughly balanced before it is turned.
options.misconception: mistakes the working sequence for a question of balance

questions.explanation: Each stage of working removes the marks of the stage before it, so the tools must become finer in turn and a coarse cut made late would undo the polish. A skin, the grain and the balance of the block are not the reason.
questions.hint: Think about what a coarse tool does to a polished surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate total work from a stepped rate
questions.stem: The clerk's note on exhibit 21 records that the carver made 18 cuts in the first hour and 26 in each of the next two hours. How many cuts had been made after three hours?

options.text: Seventy-eight cuts, since the later hours have been averaged rather than added.
options.misconception: averages the hours instead of adding them

options.text: Fifty-two cuts, since only the two later hours have been counted.
options.misconception: omits the first hour from the count

options.text: Eighty cuts, since the first hour's 18 cuts have been counted as 26.
options.misconception: applies the later rate to the first hour as well

options.text: Seventy cuts, since 26 plus 26 plus the first hour's 18 comes to 70.

questions.explanation: Adding the three hours gives 18 plus 26 plus 26, which is 70 cuts in all. The first hour was lighter because the carver was still establishing the form of the block.
questions.hint: Add the three hours, using the right figure for each.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a restorer reads a crack pattern
questions.stem: A question in the file asks how a restorer reads the crack pattern of a panel before deciding what to do. Explain what the pattern is read for.

answer.exemplar: The pattern is read to tell whether the fault is in the support or in the paint layer alone, and whether the movement is general or confined to one place. Fine cracks that cross the grain and follow the joints between boards point to the timber moving as a whole, while cracks that open in the paint film but not in the ground point to a local fault. The reading then decides whether the panel needs a new stretcher and reground or only local treatment.

questions.explanation: The pattern is read to separate a fault of the support from a fault of the surface and to see whether the movement is general or local, and that reading decides the treatment. The pattern alone never settles timing or responsibility.
questions.hint: Think about which part of the work the crack stops in.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a ratio between a ceiling field and its figures
questions.stem: A file note on a ceiling records that the painted compartment measures 9 metres across its short side and that the figures at the far end of that side are painted 1.5 metres tall. What is the ratio of the compartment's short side to the height of such a figure?
questions.explanation: The short side of 9 metres divided by the 1.5 metre height of the figure gives a ratio of 6. The large difference shows how steeply the ceiling is seen and how strongly the figures are foreshortened.
questions.hint: Divide the length of the side by the height of the figure.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tacking margins of a stretched canvas
questions.learningObjective: Interpret slack margins correctly in a file note

stimulus.body: File note on exhibit 13: the clerk records that the canvas is secured to the stretcher with tacks driven at intervals along the edges, that the painted area stops well short of the line of tacks, and that a restorer has found the unpainted edges to be slack and free of any sign of cracking or tension.

questions.stem: How should the clerk describe the slack edges recorded in the note?

options.text: As evidence that the tacks were never driven in far enough to hold the canvas.
options.misconception: blames the tacks for the slackness of the margins

options.text: As the untensioned margins that take up the movement of the support and keep the strain off the paint.
As evidence that the canvas was cut too large for the stretcher it was made for.
options.misconception: invents a mismatch between canvas and stretcher

options.text: As evidence that the picture was made to be displayed loose rather than stretched.
options.misconception: claims the picture was intended to hang unstretched

questions.explanation: The note records an unpainted edge that is slack and free of strain, which is exactly what a working margin should be. Loose tacks, an oversized canvas and an intention to hang loose would each be faults the note does not report.
questions.hint: Ask whether the slackness is a fault or a provision.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a photographic record establishes and what it depends on
questions.stem: A note describes the photographic record of an exhibit. First say what the exposure fixed, then say what the record still depends on for its weight as evidence.

options.text: It fixed the truth of the dispute, and it still depends on the strength of the lens that was used.
options.misconception: claims the plate settles the dispute and doubts the lens

options.text: It fixed the date of the object itself, and it still depends on the opinions of the person who took it.
options.misconception: claims the plate dates the object and doubts its honesty

options.text: It fixed the appearance of the object at a stated moment, and it still depends on being linked to that object and its circumstances declared.
It fixed the identity of the maker of the object, and it still depends on the chain of custody of the plate.
options.misconception: claims the plate identifies the artist and focuses on custody alone

questions.explanation: An exposure fixes how the object looked at a stated moment, and as evidence that record still has to be tied to the object and its circumstances declared. It does not date the object, settle the dispute or identify the maker.
questions.hint: Ask what the plate records and what the court still has to be told.
